title: A SIP Isnt Enough
author: Mr. Nickhart
summary: Mr. Nickhart argues that a School Improvement Plan (SIP) is not the starting point for school improvement planning -- it is the output of a prior, more fundamental question: what is our theory of change? Before deciding what goes on a plan, leaders need views on what kind of thing a school is, how they can reliably know reality, how improvement happens, and how to choose what to focus on. Drawing on complexity science, Nickhart argues that schools are complex adaptive systems where outcomes emerge unpredictably from conditions rather than being produced directly by actions -- meaning school improvement is a 'wicked problem' with no linear cause-and-effect. A plan without a theory of change is a collection of data fields with no coherent logic connecting them.
points: A School Improvement Plan is not the starting point for school improvement planning -- it is the output of a prior question: what is our theory of change? A plan without a theory is a collection of data fields with no coherent logic connecting them.

Schools are complex adaptive systems where outcomes emerge unpredictably from conditions, not produced directly by actions -- meaning there is no linear cause-and-effect, a small change can ripple unpredictably, and a large intervention can produce no effect.

A theory of change must address four questions before a plan is written: what is the nature of the reality of schools, how can we reliably know that reality, how does improvement happen, and how do we choose what to focus on.

Because schools are wicked problems -- where solving one problem changes the nature of another and every attempt to improve reveals new complexity -- improvement planning must be adaptive rather than linear.

When the upstream theory-of-change work is not done, coherence defaults to individuals who carry the system in their heads until they leave, making the organization fragile and improvement dependent on person rather than structure.
quotes: The previous posts in this series established three things. Schools are complex systems in which outcomes emerge unpredictably rather than being produced directly by actions. Planning for emergence means shifting attention upstream towards the conditions that make better patterns more likely.

A SIP isn't enough. It's not the starting point for school improvement planning. The way that it is organised and the content of it should reflect the beliefs, assumptions and evidence firstly for how schools improve but more importantly how this school improves.

A theory of change settles addresses those issues first. It is not the same as a plan. The plan records what we will do and is part of the theory of change. The theory of change explains the bigger picture within which the plan sits. Without the theory, the plan is a collection of data fields with no coherent logic connecting them.
Schools are complex adaptive systems; networks of people, relationships and beliefs that interact in ways that cannot be fully predicted or controlled.

School improvement is a wicked problem: parts of the school are interdependent, solving one problem changes the nature of another and every attempt to improve reveals new complexity.
